lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Owned the pick-path layouts for the fast-moving zone and the labor reports the shift leads used.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; the findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.

- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations while also covering night-shift supervision, updating the safety training slides, coordinating holiday temp hiring and running the forklift certification schedule, which raised inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5%.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Reduced freight costs by 15% by consolidating supplier pickups into regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.
- Built the weekly supplier scorecard for 40 vendors, which buyers used to renegotiate delivery windows with the five least reliable.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Cut average order lead time through the warehouse from 10 days to 5 while holding daily throughput constant and doubling work-in-process to keep pickers busy.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Checked the planned routes against 4 weeks of real delivery logs; planned drive times came within 5% of the actual ones.
- Shared the model and a one-page summary with the grocer's dispatch team, who piloted the routes on two trucks for a month.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Built a seasonal forecast for 1,400 products across three warehouses that more than halved stockouts and cut inventory by nearly $2M.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Put the experience entries in reverse chronological order, with Crestway before Lakeview.
items.because: The current order makes the work history look out of sequence.

items.says: Move Education below Experience.
items.because: With several years of relevant work history, the results are likely more persuasive than the degree at the top.

items.says: Make the target role clearer and give more space to relevant experience.
items.because: The strongest evidence is in supply chain, planning, and distribution operations, while the florist job is less relevant.

items.says: Replace any placeholder contact details with real details and a working professional profile link.
items.because: A literal example-domain email or URL will look unfinished.

items.says: Check that the profile URL is clickable and its page is current and consistent with the résumé.
Clarify what the 30–40-arrangement daily volume represents.
items.because: It is unclear whether it is typical volume, a range across shifts, or a peak.

items.says: Give the payment duty less emphasis unless it involved notable responsibility or results.
items.because: Taking payment is routine.

items.says: Clarify your contribution to the wedding orders and the scale of the orders.
items.because: The bullet otherwise reads mostly as a list of general shop duties.

items.says: Prioritize a relevant quality, accuracy, or waste result over routine tasks if one is available.
items.because: The wedding-order work is more distinctive than keeping the cooler stocked and labeled.

items.says: Specify what you changed or maintained and how broad the responsibility was.
items.because: “Owned” leaves the scope unclear.

items.says: Show what the layouts or reports helped improve.
items.because: The bullet describes ownership without showing a result.

items.says: Define “processing time” and explain how the three-day and one-day figures were measured.
items.because: That would make the size and reliability of the improvement easier to assess.

items.says: Give the measurement period or clarify the averages compared for trailer wait.
items.because: The reader needs to understand the before-and-after figures and your contribution.

items.says: Separate the inventory result from the other duties or remove lower-value duties.
items.because: The bullet combines too many responsibilities and is hard to scan.

items.says: Clarify how cycle counting contributed to the accuracy increase.
items.because: The current construction makes the cause difficult to follow.

items.says: Clarify the time period and basis for the stockout comparison.
Explain what the $1.9 million inventory reduction represents.
items.because: A reduction in inventory value should not be presented as cash savings unless that is what it was.

items.says: Specify your role in developing or implementing the forecast model.
Distinguish this forecast result from the similar food-bank claim.
items.because: Both describe about 1,400 products across three facilities, a major stockout reduction, and nearly $2 million less inventory.

items.says: State the period and comparison basis for the 15% freight-cost reduction.
items.because: Without a baseline, the reader cannot judge its significance.

items.says: Give the scale of the freight operation if it can be substantiated.
Connect the reorder-point work to a supported outcome or explain its scale and implementation.
items.because: The bullet describes a responsibility but gives no outcome.

items.says: Distinguish the reorder-point work from the forecasting contribution.
items.because: The two bullets may overlap.

items.says: Explain what changed after buyers renegotiated the delivery windows, if measurable.
items.because: The scorecard’s use is clear, but its effect is not.

items.says: Clarify the basis for calling the five vendors “least reliable.”
The stated 112% OEE needs correction or an accurate metric label.
items.because: Standard OEE is generally capped at 100%, so the figure raises questions about the calculation or definition.

items.says: Define what “order lead time” covers.
Explain the operational change and whether doubling WIP had downsides.
items.because: Higher WIP may be a costly tradeoff, suggesting the shorter lead time came at the expense of inventory or efficiency.

items.says: Clarify your relationship with the grocer and your personal role.
items.because: The independent-project label and later pilot together suggest an external client engagement.

items.says: Make clear that the grocer’s anonymous description is deliberate if the client cannot be named.
Define the comparison behind the 18% route-mile reduction, including stops and operating constraints.
items.because: That would make the result more credible.

items.says: Explain what “planned drive times” refers to.
Explain how the four weeks of delivery logs were used.
items.because: The validation method is vague.

items.says: Report actual pilot results if available, or clarify what the pilot established.
Clarify whether the project is still active.
Distinguish your individual contribution from the team’s work.
items.because: “Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4” does not make it clear.

items.says: Clarify what Excel was used for.
items.because: The tool label alone is not very informative.

items.says: Replace the general analysis bullet with a concrete contribution or remove it.
items.because: It is broad and adds little beyond the more specific bullets.

items.says: Clarify your role in mapping and removing the data-entry steps.
items.because: The passive phrasing makes it hard to tell who implemented the change.

items.says: Explain how the one-day improvement was measured.
Resolve the apparent similarity to the Crestway forecast result, distinguishing the setting and measures if this is separate work.
items.because: Both claims describe about 1,400 products across three facilities, a major stockout reduction, and nearly $2 million less inventory.

items.says: Specify your own contribution to the team’s forecasting work.
Add other relevant systems, software, or analytical tools actually used.
items.because: Excel and Python alone may underrepresent your capabilities for planning and operations roles.

items.says: Clarify proficiency if it varies substantially between tools.
Better reflect the methods behind the major improvements shown in Experience.
items.because: The listed methods do not fully reflect that work.
